research_tasks: Research log (2026-10-22, first run, mode create, empty baseline-reader.md, no prior evidence, no research notes file in docs/content-analysis/research/). No existing draft, page or research brief for Josh Hartnett was found under any name in src/blog/people/drafts or docs/content-analysis/research, and no public Enneagram typing was found. Not open-case eligible: his career began in 1997 and the record runs 1999-2026, so this is a standard profile. Opened 30 sources (S01-S30) and recorded 7 unopened (S31-S37). Read in full: the 2002 Observer (S03), 2003 Philstar junket (S04), 2020 Guardian (S02), 2021 Mr Porter (S07), 2024 Observer (S01), 2024 Interview conversation with Julia Stiles (S08), 2024 Hollywood Authentic (S12), 2026 NPR (S14), 2026 The Film Stage (S15), 2026 Sharp (S16) and 2026 Hollywood Reporter (S19), plus local transcripts of two full CBC Q interviews (2024 and 2026, about 47 minutes, S11, S18) and a 2018 red-carpet clip (S20). Evidence was gathered before choosing a type. A Six reading formed from the 2020 Guardian fear calculus and was then tested against the 2002 Observer (the strongest Nine evidence) and the 2024-2026 interviews, which it survived at medium confidence. Outcome: status ready, standard format, Type 6 at medium confidence, Type 9 the strongest rival, Types 4 and 7 live; contested_typing and sensitive_allegations are flagged so the six-role jury reviews it.

Transcript fidelity. S11 and S18 (CBC Q podcast audio from the public RSS feed, cbc.ca/podcasting/includes/qpodcast.xml) and S20 (YouTube, downloaded with yt-dlp using the mweb client) were transcribed locally with whisper.cpp medium.en and checked against small.en. The excerpts agree in wording across both models, but punctuation, repeated words and fillers are machine-made. Re-listen at the listed timestamps (they include pre-roll ads) before printing any verbatim quote from these three sources; for 2024 Q quotes prefer CBC's edited text (S10). Scratch files (may not survive to later stages): audio and transcripts in /tmp/jh-research/qpod/ and /tmp/jh-research/yt_anx/, page texts in /tmp/jh-research/<source>/page.txt. Every excerpt in this file was machine-checked against those saved texts before writing (0 mismatches).

Access workarounds and independence. S07 (Mr Porter; 403 and the reader proxy blocked) and S05 (Evening Chronicle) were opened through Wayback raw captures (web.archive.org/web/<year>id_/<url>). S08 (Interview) was opened through r.jina.ai. Toronto Life's 2026 interview returned a CAPTCHA and was not used. Not independent: S10 is an edited write-up of S11; S23-S26, S29 and S30 compile or report other interviews; Today.com, Just Jared, E!, Complex, AV Club, Fox News and Far Out repackage S01 and S02 and were not used as corroboration.

Handling and do-not-use list. (1) Sensitive: the man with a gun at a premiere who "ended up in prison" (C33) is his unverified account; attribute it, add nothing, name no one. His mother's drug and alcohol problems, dementia and 2023 death (S01) are disclosures about a deceased private person: omit, or one attributed sentence with no causal claim. The crash fault ("a police car running a red light", C45) is his allegation; police said they were investigating. Weinstein (C24): keep his words; do not imply he alleges abuse. (2) Do not name or gender his children (kept private, S29). (3) Do not repeat the 1998-2002 tabloid sex rumours in S26 or name past girlfriends. (4) Do not write that he turned down Batman (C12) or that Superman was worth $100m (C11). (5) Do not use the Harrison Ford "hated him" quote (C18). (6) Say "asked to leave" Purchase, not "expelled" (C07); "played with Al Green's touring band", not "Al Green's guitarist" (C03); "about a year and a half" for the break, not a month count (C19); "as a teenager" for the knee injury (C05). (7) "Suffers from anxiety" overstates S20; it was stage nerves (C35). (8) "A natural worrier" is McGurk's phrase, not Hartnett's (C34). (9) Avoid partisan framing of his Obama and Biden remarks (S01).

Unopened or set aside. Could not open: Details 2014 (S31), Playboy 2015 (S32), the 2001 Vanity Fair profile (S33), Rolling Stone 1999 (S34), HuffPost 2017 (S35), USA Today 2015 (S36) and Men's Health 2024 (S37); their quotes are known only through secondary pages and are marked as such in C12, C21, C28, C30 and C48. Also not opened: the Happy Sad Confused audio with Nolan (reported by CNN, S21), Shyamalan's GQ video (reported by TheWrap, S22), Empire podcasts #439 (2020) and #629 (2024), the 2021 Sunrise interview, and Fight or Flight (2025) press. None is essential to the type argument; S31 and S32 would strengthen or weaken the distrust and pigeonholing quotes.

Draft-stage leads. Internal links among existing drafts: Christopher-Nolan (5), Christian-Bale (5), Cillian-Murphy (5), Ben-Affleck (3), Anne-Hathaway (1), dakota-johnson (4) and Jake-Gyllenhaal (6, same-type contrast) are published; Keanu-Reeves (9, published) and Brendan-Fraser (9, unpublished) are the obvious "walked away from Hollywood" comparisons and should be distinguished, not echoed. For the next refresh: (a) any account of how he handled a collaborator who let him down, or a public conflict, where Six and Nine part most clearly; (b) what he says steadied him through the Verity/Below release week he called "terrifying" (credits trusted people and preparation, Six; tuning it all out, Nine); (c) the Oliver Stone film's title (White Lies per S15), release and his account of it (C37); (d) the 2014 Details and 2015 Playboy originals; (e) any RNC finding on the September 2025 crash (C45); (f) any Below season-two decision (C44).

sources.title: 'I didn't want to be swallowed up': actor Josh Hartnett on swapping Hollywood for Hampshire
sources.speaker: Josh Hartnett, interviewed over Zoom by Stuart McGurk (The Observer magazine, published on theguardian.com); includes M. Night Shyamalan quoted on casting him
sources.locator: Full feature, amended 28 July 2024. Paragraphs: the Hampshire morning routine and the 180-day marriage visa; the 18-month stop and Superman "twice"; "swinging for something"; Shyamalan on casting; the Nolan/Prestige history and Oppenheimer call; childhood in Saint Paul ("existentialist from the age of 12"); his mother; his father's four-day week; the stalking and premiere-gun account; politics; The Bear and "his new rule".
sources.excerpt: In reality, Hartnett only stopped working for 18 months. [...] (He notably turned down the role of Superman twice.) “I just didn’t want my life to be swallowed up by my work,” he says now. “And there was a notion at that time you just kind of give it all up. And you saw what happened to some people back then. They got obliterated by it. I didn’t want that for myself.” [...] “Some of those films were successful. Some of them were failures. But I was always swinging for something that was outside what people expected from me.” [...] “And so to find somebody that’s a bona fide movie star, that’s a great human being and is willing to risk everything, man, that’s a rare combination. And sometimes you think that doesn’t exist any more. And then he walked in.” [...] “But the implication was: ‘I’d better take it.’ You only get so many opportunities with Chris Nolan.” [...] “I recognise the missed opportunity to work with a guy like Chris. And I’ve figured out that as much as you’re worried about curating your career to things you’re interested in, I don’t believe that’s the most important thing any more. It’s about finding people who you really trust.” [...] A natural worrier (“My family says I was an existentialist from the age of 12”) and lover of the arts, but also a jock who played on the school football team. [...] “My dad was not someone who valued achievement in that way – high-level work achievement as a means of proving himself. He owned a company. He allowed himself and his employees to work four days a week. And he was home a lot.” [...] “People’s attention to me at the time was borderline unhealthy.” [...] “Well, look, I don’t want to give this a lot of weight,” he begins. [...] “There were incidents. People showed up at my house. People that were stalking me.” At one point, he says, “a guy showed up at one of my premieres with a gun, claiming to be my father. He ended up in prison.” Harnett was 27 at the time – this was 19 years ago. “There were lots of things. It was a weird time. And I wasn’t going to be grist for the mill.” [...] It was, after all, his new rule: work with people you trust. [...] He’s in the UK on a marriage visa, which means he can only be out of the country for work 180 days a year, or roughly one movie, which also suits him fine. [...] In a way, less is happening. But more of the important stuff is happening.
sources.context: Long-form Observer interview for Trap; the richest recent source on family and the retreat. Writer framing to keep attributed: "A natural worrier" is McGurk's paraphrase introducing Hartnett's family quote; "what he's about to say is a reason, not to be confused with the reason" is McGurk's gloss on the stalking story; "his new rule: work with people you trust" is McGurk's summary. Also in the piece: his parents were hippies in a "shared living situation" ("I'm not going to say it was a commune"); they split, his mother moved to San Francisco, and by the time he was four his father had married his stepmother, an artist from whom he got painting; he worked at the video store Mr Movies. His mother: "No, she died last year" (July 2024), "We had spent most of my youth not around each other. And she had issues with drugs and alcohol"; she later developed dementia. That is sensitive health information about a deceased private person; see research_tasks. Factual slips in this source: it says Nolan was working on The Dark Knight when they spoke (Nolan, S21, ties the conversation to his Batman casting, i.e. Batman Begins, 2005), and the subject's name is misspelled "Harnett" twice. He says he campaigned for Obama and voices fear that democracy "might not be able to withstand those shocks" (July 2024, days after the attempt on Trump).

sources.title: Josh Hartnett: 'People genuinely thought I'd been thrust on them'
sources.speaker: Josh Hartnett, interviewed over Zoom from Surrey by Ryan Gilbey (The Guardian), plus a follow-up phone call
sources.locator: Full feature for Target Number One. Paragraphs: the Superman "fear-based character" idea; Michael Bay's "fucking huge"; meeting Victor Malarek; Dimension/Weinstein contract extensions; Pearl Harbor decision; the 2001 Vanity Fair piece; studio fallout and "burned my bridges"; Batman; the follow-up call about Weinstein; re-reading Vanity Fair ("tallest poppy").
sources.excerpt: “I had this idea that because he lives in this world where he can’t touch anything without it flying across the room, he has become almost afraid of himself and his own power. He doesn’t know how to be Superman any more. [...] The studio demurred – “They didn’t really want a fear-based character at the centre of their movie,” he says wryly – and Hartnett walked away. [...] Michael Bay, who directed him in Pearl Harbor, put it bluntly: “He’s going to be fucking huge.” The actor grimaces at the mention of that. “Huge was never something I aspired to,” he says. [...] Naturally he met with the real Malarek before playing him. Why? “I wanted to see if he was full of shit.” [...] “My interest in going to meet him was not to have flowers laid at my feet.” [...] “We had a sort of antagonistic relationship because the contract I signed for those first two films guaranteed me to be a part of, like, five more or something. [...] He shifts uneasily when I ask whether he was surprised by the revelations about Harvey Weinstein. [...] When he was offered Pearl Harbor, his instinct was to turn it down. “I didn’t necessarily want things to change that much,” he says. “I was happy with the amount of fame I had and the types of roles I was getting. At the same time, I asked myself: ‘Am I just afraid that by doing Pearl Harbor, I’m going to enter a new category of film-making that I might not be ready for?’ I ultimately chose to do it because turning it down would’ve been based on fear. Then it defined me, which means I was right to fear it.” [...] “Oh, that was an awful piece,” he shudders. “Was there even a quote from me in it, or was it just everyone talking about how hot I was? People got a chip on their shoulder about me after that. They genuinely thought I’d been thrust on them. It was a very weird time.” [...] After Superman, there were reports that he had also turned down Batman; in fact, he didn’t get any closer to that part than a conversation with Christopher Nolan. [...] “They looked at me as someone who had bitten the hand that fed me. It wasn’t that. I wasn’t doing it to be recalcitrant or a rebel. People wanted to create a brand around me that was going to be accessible and well-liked, but I didn’t respond to the idea of playing the same character over and over, so I branched out. I tried to find smaller films I could be part of and, in the process, I burned my bridges at the studios because I wasn’t participating. Our goals weren’t the same.” [...] He is nothing if not conscientious. A few days after our Zoom conversation, he phones me because something has been bothering him: he doesn’t feel he made his feelings about Weinstein clear. This time, he puts it as plainly as he can. “I wasn’t surprised he was a creep,” he says. “But I guess I was surprised at the extent of his creepiness.” [...] “That’s not my experience and it’s not my place to claim that. It makes me feel icky to try to do so.” [...] I felt like: ‘Oh my God! I’m not the tallest poppy yet – don’t cut me down!’ I was being compared to Tom Cruise and Julia Roberts and that’s insane. It was a set-up-to-fail moment.” He gives a sigh. “It was actually an interesting look at the nature of fame. If only it wasn’t about me.”
sources.context: The most revealing single interview on the 2001-2004 decisions, with an observed behaviour (the unprompted follow-up call) reported by the writer. Interpretive lines are Gilbey's: the Superman concept "now feels like a metaphor for what was happening at the time in his own life"; "It was around then that he plotted his calculated retreat"; "He is nothing if not conscientious". The Weinstein material is about a convicted sex offender; Hartnett explicitly declines to claim he was harassed. Also here: he does his homework (raked over Trip Fontaine with Jeffrey Eugenides; trained as a boxer for months for The Black Dahlia); Dimension (Miramax) exercised contract extensions and became co-producer on O and Lucky Number Slevin; he and Tamsin Egerton moved to Surrey to be near her parents. Not independent of: Today.com, Just Jared, E! and El País (S24) reuse these quotes.

sources.title: Hart throb
sources.speaker: Josh Hartnett, interviewed in a New York hotel during the 40 Days and 40 Nights junket by Rachel Cooke (The Observer); includes Sofia Coppola and Ben Affleck quoted
sources.locator: Full feature. Paragraphs: the hotel meeting ("gauche and anxious"); Twin Cities home; parents "hippyish"; how he fell into acting; Pearl Harbor ("I nearly turned it down"); Tom Cruise comparison; the "blank space" theory of fame; Sean Penn and the "bullshit meter"; "go along for the ride"; time off; "turn right, go left"; the publicity machine.
sources.excerpt: he walks into the room looking so gauche and anxious and unbelievably handsome that it's hard to sit still. [...] His folks are, he insists, are a lot more interested in achieving happiness rather than success - and brought Josh up to be just the same way. [...] 'You just knew he had it,' she said. [...] 'Yeah, I nearly turned it down,' he says, though he clearly dislikes talking about the film which, in relation to the expectations heaped on it, turned out to be a Titanic-sized flop. 'It was a role a lot of people wanted but... I didn't want to be famous.' [...] He looks uncomfortable. 'I dunno. Tom Cruise is a multinational corporation.' He pauses and then, perhaps afraid that he might sound as if he is dissing Cruise, adds: [...] 'Yes, by realising I'm not any more important than anyone else. [...] He stops, looks flustered, runs his hands through his hair. 'I'm just coming up with this theory right now, so tell me if it's bullshit. [...] People care about my fame, not me. But that's fine. I have my own life. [...] 'I respect people who recognise their boundaries as to how much of this stuff they can take. I also respect people who can work in the midst of this press bonanza. Luckily, I've got a pretty good bullshit meter. I'm pretty good at returning to life after my work is done.' [...] 'I just kind go along for the ride. You need some people in the world who are determined to do one thing in life, to make that thing their goal. But luckily, because you have all those other people being pillars, holding up the world, someone like me can just wander through.' [...] 'It's completely down to me. These guys give me suggestions, obviously, but I'm one of those people who when someone says "turn right," go left. I don't know whether they've figured that out yet...' [...] 'You know, I'm not interested in fighting the publicity machine,' he says. 'That's not my fight. There are other things I want to fight for. I want interesting roles. I want to do some good in the world.'
sources.context: The only long contemporaneous interview from the peak (age 23) that was opened. Cooke's tone is arch and flirtatious; her readings ("perhaps afraid", "though I am not entirely sure I believe him", "Poor boy. He'll learn, I guess") are interpretation and must stay attributed. Facts here: he still lived in the Twin Cities; parents divorced, close to both; three younger siblings; father had played guitar for Al Green "before taking over the family real estate business" (but see C03: in 2026 he narrowed this); knee injury "at 16" (S04 says 15); first role in Cracker; Ben Affleck to Vanity Fair: "He is so very pretty". NPR (S14) read him this piece's "date" line in 2026. Wikipedia (S27) cites this article as the archived Observer piece.

sources.title: Into the heart of Josh
sources.speaker: Josh Hartnett at a Hollywood Homicide press round table at the Four Seasons, Beverly Hills, reported by Ricky Lo (The Philippine Star)
sources.locator: Round-table junket held "several weeks" before publication (the film opened in the US in June 2003). Passages: Huck Finn; SUNY Purchase letter to the dean; Harrison Ford; Minneapolis vs Los Angeles; Superman.
sources.excerpt: "Yes, that’s the person I’ve always wanted to be, somebody like Huck Finn. Somebody who’s not always accepted by society but who finds his own ideals and isn’t afraid to go out on a limb." [...] "I objected to the school’s practice of admitting more students than it would ultimately graduate and felt that the program’s highly competitive structure stifled students’ creativity. Instead of writing an essay for one of my liberal arts classes, I decided to take the opportunity to speak my mind. I wrote a letter to the dean and to my teachers about the policy. They didn’t appreciate it, so they asked me to leave. I stayed in that school for only five months." [...] He’s my idol. It was a little bit intimidating at first but eventually we got along very well. [...] "I feel more comfortable there. I come to Hollywood to work and then I go back to Minneapolis where I can be myself. [...] You’re either an outsider looking in or an insider stuck inside this expensive ball of wax. [...] I asked myself, ‘Am I going to feel fulfilled doing this?’ The answer was no. Probably not. I just felt that putting on the tights just didn’t make sense. [...] "I think more than anything physical, it’s my drive to explore things, my desire to experience the world. [...] Sitting there at the round table, being grilled by the journalists, Josh looked like a schoolboy taking an oral exam.
sources.context: A shared junket round table, so his answers were given to a dozen outlets at once; treat as his on-record words, not an exclusive. The writer gives his birth date as July 21, 1978, says he broke his knee "when he was 15" (S03 and S07 say 16) and that he was "kicked out due to his, yes, 'rebel streak'" (writer's phrase). His own account of the Purchase exit is the most detailed available; compare S26 (Rolling Stone 1999 via AnOther) and S24.

sources.title: He'll stay out of limelight
sources.speaker: Josh Hartnett, quoted in an unbylined Evening Chronicle (Newcastle) feature for Wicker Park
sources.locator: Opened via the Wayback raw capture web.archive.org/web/20160614184102id_/ (the live URL is the one Wikipedia cites). Paragraphs on the hottest-actor poll, the 15 months out, painting, Superman, Wicker Park.
sources.excerpt: "I'm absolutely not in the race to be the hottest actor," he insists. "I know what it's like to be in that whole world. I was up there for a couple of years and it was uncomfortable. [...] "I think trying to stay at the top is a shortcut to unhappiness." [...] "I spent a bit of time really thinking about whether this was the right thing for me," he reveals. "I took 15 months out of the business. I was like a lot of people in their 20s, wondering, 'Who am I? What do I want to be when I grow up?'. [...] I always wanted to be a painter and if I had the means I might just hermit myself away and do that for a while." [...] "I didn't ever want to do it," he explains. "It just wasn't the kind of movie I wanted to do. I turned down other superhero roles as well."
sources.context: Probably junket copy syndicated to regional papers; no interviewer named. The only near-contemporaneous source for the length of the break, which he gives as 15 months; McGurk (S01) and El País (S24) say 18 months. Writer calls him "introspective" and notes he is rarely seen at showbiz parties and had just bought a home in Minnesota.

sources.title: 'Penny Dreadful' actor Josh Hartnett discusses his role on the Victorian TV show
sources.speaker: Josh Hartnett, interviewed by Lynn Elber (Associated Press), published by The Christian Science Monitor
sources.locator: AP feature for Penny Dreadful season 1; the paragraphs on release guarantees, 2001 fame, "the narrative ... that I disappeared", and "Being 35 and not 18".
sources.excerpt: Hartnett also appreciated the guarantee that the project would be marketed and presented to an audience, something he's become painfully aware isn't always the case with independent films. [...] "It's really exciting to have a big movie release," said Hartnett. "Everybody should be so lucky to have that experience. You feel like the whole world's focused on you for a little while, and it's overwhelming." [...] "The narrative that's been created over the last couple months is that I disappeared, and I was some hermit for the last few years and joined a cult or something," he said. "It's just crazy. ... I was doing work I thought was worthy." [...] "Being 35 and not 18, I'm less susceptible to the negative aspects"
sources.context: AP wire copy, so it ran in many papers; this is one copy, not independent corroboration of anything else. The "guarantee" sentence is the writer's paraphrase of his reasons for doing TV.

sources.title: Why Mr Josh Hartnett Chose "Having A Life" Over The Hollywood Dream
sources.speaker: Josh Hartnett, interviewed on a video call in mid-December 2020 by Alex Bilmes (MR PORTER, The Journal)
sources.locator: Opened via the Wayback raw capture web.archive.org/web/2021id_/ (live site returned 403). Published January 2021 per syndicated reports; interview conducted mid-December 2020. Passages: Superman; the chewing-gum anecdote; "I decided to have a life"; becoming "a commodity"; "terrified that someone's coming up behind them"; friends and family; Minneapolis; "I would not have a happy life".
sources.excerpt: “At the time, it was so obvious to me to turn it down,” says the actor in his measured Midwestern baritone. “I was being offered movies by the very top directors. And Superman was a risk. Yes, there was a lot of money involved, but I didn’t think that was the be-all and end-all.” [...] There was a time I was considered quite a commodity in the business and I wanted my character to chew gum in a scene. It was run up so many flagpoles and it was the subject of conversation for days and in the end, they decided just no. [...] “I decided to have a life,” says Mr Hartnett. “To put that first. That was always my goal.” [...] “I started to realise that I had to perform in a certain way in the marketplace or I was going to lose my career,” says Mr Hartnett. [...] “The guys who are on top are terrified that someone’s coming up behind them. If that’s your real ambition, to be on top all the time, you’re going to spend your whole life looking over your shoulder. I never wanted that. I want to do good work with people I like and spend my free time with people I care about.” [...] “I’m not going to speak for other people,” he says, choosing his words carefully, [...] “A lot of people get caught in that trap, but I feel very strongly about friends I’ve known for a long time and my family. I wanted to make sure I wasn’t losing those relationships. Those people make me who I am. I put those concerns ahead of chasing a Hollywood dream.” [...] “People thought I was crazy for not chasing that brass ring a little harder,” he says, “but I felt completely comfortable being with the people I knew liked me before I was making films. [...] but I will say that in giving in to the allure of Hollywood entirely, I know that I would not have a happy life,” he says. “I feel very strongly about that.”
sources.context: He raised Superman himself ("every interviewer asks me about it"). The $100m three-film fee is "according to industry gossip" (writer); do not state it as fact. Writer's framing: the decision "to prioritise relationships with friends and family over those with industry powerbrokers ... personal values of honesty and integrity". Also: three children then (born by end of 2019), living on the Surrey-Sussex border; at 16 he "tore his anterior cruciate ligament"; "College had lasted all of six months". El País (S24) and others reuse these quotes.

sources.title: Josh Hartnett Tells Julia Stiles How He Escaped the Hollywood Trap
sources.speaker: Josh Hartnett in conversation with Julia Stiles, his O co-star (Interview magazine, September 2024 issue)
sources.locator: Transcript dated "MONDAY 7 PM JUNE 25, 2024 LONDON"; opened via r.jina.ai. Passages: leaving L.A. ("just plain sanity"), community, returning to studio films, Trap, method acting, goats, press comfort.
sources.excerpt: But the choice to step back from the industry had more to do with just plain sanity. In the late ’90s and early 2000s, as you remember, if you were named as one of these interesting people in celebrity culture, it was then the press’s mission to tear you apart. [...] I wanted to be myself amongst people that I knew, so I was able to revert back to my family and friends in Minnesota. Also, after a certain amount of time chasing a goal, I realized that achieving these things wasn’t giving me back the satisfaction I hoped it would, so I had to find something else to fill that gap. I felt, and still feel, that community is what fills it. Achievement is great in any walk of life. It’s a reason to get up in the morning. But the thing that really holds you is your community. I felt that I was kind of rootless at that time, so I wanted to find that community. [...] But coming back to making studio films, what happened in all transparency was that we had a couple of kids, so I wanted to establish something that was a little bit more solid. [...] You and I both had attention that we didn’t know how to navigate. [...] I think method acting is a joke that some actor came up with. [...] So we got some goats to deal with that. The goats are more my vibe. [...] But I like being the outlier. [...] But when you’re very young, it’s like you’re trying to find yourself, and the world is telling you what they think you are, and it’s discombobulating. So you’re forced to either fight against or go along with people’s perceptions of you.
sources.context: A peer conversation rather than a profile, so it shows his register with a friend: warm, joking, self-deprecating. Stiles' line is her own testimony about the O cast's shared experience, not an observation of him specifically. He says he "never really lived in L.A." (he lived "set to set" and in Minnesota and New York). Tamsin Egerton: met playing husband and wife in "the worst movie either of us have ever made" in London, both left other partners, she got pregnant, then they married. Four children; "I'm a foreigner in my own home" (joke about an English family). On method actors: "To make the whole set focus on and be afraid of them".

sources.title: Can't You Just Let Josh Hartnett Be an Indie Weirdo?
sources.speaker: Josh Hartnett, interviewed at the Crosby Street Hotel, Manhattan, by Brittany Spanos (Rolling Stone)
sources.locator: Feature for Trap; the quoted passages on career path, weird characters and the "treadmill", the frontal-lobe line, and his kids.
sources.excerpt: “I was never a person that had a career path in mind or wanted to be the biggest movie star in the world,” Hartnett says, sitting in Manhattan’s Crosby Street Hotel. “That wasn’t who I ever was. So it wasn’t like I stepped away, it was just that people had an idea of what I could be. And I was never feeling that way.” [...] “It’s so much easier to do things within this business when you’re a little bit older,” he says, “because you’re not worried about other people defining you to the public in a way that you don’t feel comfortable with, because your frontal lobe is fully developed. It wasn’t when I was 20. [...] “I thought I was going to be able to continue to play weird characters or characters that were outside of the heroic archetypes. And after certain movies came out, the studios or whoever was in charge wanted me to stay on that treadmill. But I just continued doing my own thing, and it was hard. [...] “I’ve never made a movie that’s for young audiences, and my kids don’t really understand what I do,” he admits.
sources.context: Writer's framing: "Josh Hartnett has always wanted to do what was least expected of him." Also: he met Kid Cudi at a 2009 Ratatat concert and directed the "Pursuit of Happiness" video for about five grand (Wikipedia says produced); he hopes to work with the Coen brothers and Scorsese.

sources.title: Josh Hartnett on escaping the heartthrob label to explore more interesting roles
sources.speaker: Vivian Rashotte (CBC Arts), quoting Hartnett from his Q with Tom Power interview
sources.locator: Article version of the Q interview (S11); the quoted paragraphs on "oddly stifling", "throw caution to the wind", and "explorative artist".
sources.excerpt: "After Pearl Harbor came out and Black Hawk Down was coming out, it felt oddly stifling," Hartnett tells Q's Tom Power in an interview. "I was both young enough and had wise enough people around me that I was able to see that … I wasn't going to be able to create my own identity in a positive way in that environment where everybody else had an opinion on what I should be." sources.excerpt: Personally, I didn’t want someone else dictating how I was portrayed in the media, and how I was portrayed on screen so much. So to have all these other opinions of who I was constantly swirling around in the miasma that is my brain while I’m trying to decide what it is that I want to be – it didn’t feel entirely healthy. [...] I think, looking back on it, it was self-protective, but it was also much more positive than that. [...] Especially when I’m not working, it feels unnatural to be constantly talking about work, or constantly talking about my own career. It feels too isolating, and it’s self-indulgent. [...] Honestly, I’ve become really fond of being here: the quiet, the still; all of it. [...] So coming to the UK didn’t feel unnatural. [...] ‘I used to track-race Porsche cars all the time. claims.claim: Josh Hartnett was born Joshua Daniel Hartnett on July 21, 1978, in Saint Paul, Minnesota.
claims.inference: Date and place from Wikipedia (S27) and the 2003 Philstar junket profile (S04). Consistent with his printed ages: 23 in April 2002 (S03), 26 in September 2004 (S05), 42 in October 2020 (S02), 46 in July 2024 (S01), 48 in October 2026 (S17, S19).
claims.alternative: None on the facts.

claims.claim: His parents, whom he describes as hippies, split when he was small; his mother moved to San Francisco, and by the time he was four his father had married his stepmother, an artist, so he was raised mainly by his father and stepmother in what he calls "a much more normal Midwestern existence".
claims.inference: His own account in 2002 ("hippyish", divorced, close to both, S03) and 2024 (S01). The 2003 writer (S04) gives the same household: father, stepmother an artist, four children. He got his love of painting from his stepmother (S01).
claims.alternative: Do not build a causal childhood story. He has never linked the split or his mother's absence to his choices; he links his values to his father (C04). His mother's addiction, dementia and 2023 death are his disclosure about a deceased private person (S01); use at most one attributed sentence, or omit.

claims.claim: His father was a musician before becoming a building manager who ran his own company; the oft-repeated description of him as a "former guitarist for Al Green" (Wikipedia's wording) overstates it: in 2026 Hartnett said his father played in Al Green's touring band around the Midwest and was not "Al Green's guy".
claims.inference: S03 (2002) and Wikipedia (S27) say guitar player for Al Green; S18 (2026, machine transcript) narrows it to touring with Green around the Midwest ("he played with Al Green one time" in Hartnett's retelling of a family question). S01: building manager, "He owned a company".
claims.alternative: Use the 2026 wording, or say he played in Al Green's touring band. Re-listen to S18 at about 12:30-13:00 before quoting.

claims.claim: He credits his father with the value that "work is never going to fulfill you in the way the family does": his father "was not someone who valued achievement in that way", owned a company and let himself and his employees work four days a week, and his family never made achievement a priority.
claims.inference: Stated in 2002 (parents "more interested in achieving happiness rather than success", S03), 2024 (S01) and 2026 (S18). It is a stable, repeated self-explanation for his low career ambition, which counts against a Three reading and is neutral between Six and Nine.
claims.alternative: Learned family value and Midwestern culture explain this without any type; it is the reason he gives, not proof of motive.

claims.claim: A high-school football player, he turned to youth theatre after a knee injury ended football (he was cast as Huck Finn in Tom Sawyer), originally wanted to be a painter, and fell for film while working at the Saint Paul video store Mr Movies.
claims.inference: Consistent across 2002, 2003, 2021 and 2024.
claims.alternative: The age of the injury conflicts: 16 (S03, S07) or 15 (S04). Say he was a teenager without giving an age.

claims.claim: In 2003 he said Huck Finn was "the person I've always wanted to be": "Somebody who's not always accepted by society but who finds his own ideals and isn't afraid to go out on a limb."
claims.inference: An early self-image as an outsider who proves he is not afraid. It fits a counterphobic Six reading (courage defined against fear) and also Four (outsider) or Seven (adventure).
claims.alternative: Junket round-table answer given to a dozen outlets; a flattering self-description, not behaviour.

claims.claim: He left SUNY Purchase's acting conservatory after a few months, after writing a letter to the dean and his teachers objecting that the programme admitted more students than it would graduate and that its competitive structure stifled creativity; accounts differ on whether he was expelled or invited to leave.
claims.inference: His fullest account (2003, S04): "They didn't appreciate it, so they asked me to leave. I stayed in that school for only five months." Rolling Stone 1999 via AnOther (S26): "they didn't really kick me out; they just said I could leave if I wanted to". Mr Porter (S07): "College had lasted all of six months." El País (S24): "expelled". At 18 he challenged an institution's evaluation system in writing: an early instance of confronting authority on principle.
claims.alternative: Writers call it a "rebel streak" (S04); a teenager's protest essay is common. Avoid "expelled"; say he was asked to leave, in his words.

claims.claim: Between 1997 and 2002 he went from the TV series Cracker to Halloween H20, The Faculty, The Virgin Suicides, Pearl Harbor, Black Hawk Down, O and 40 Days and 40 Nights, and was marketed as the next Tom Cruise.
claims.inference: Filmography from S27; the "new Tom Cruise" billing from S03 (2002) and his 2020 memory of being compared to Cruise and Julia Roberts (S02).
claims.alternative: None on the facts.

claims.claim: He nearly turned down Pearl Harbor; in 2020 he said he took it because "turning it down would've been based on fear. Then it defined me, which means I was right to fear it."
claims.inference: 2002 (S03): "Yeah, I nearly turned it down ... I didn't want to be famous." 2020 (S02): he asked himself "Am I just afraid ...?" and chose against the fear. The shape matters more than the decision: he audits his own motive for fear, acts against it, then reads the bad outcome as proof the fear was right. That is the counterphobic Six pattern; it is the single best piece of evidence for the type.
claims.alternative: Narrated 19 years later, polished by hindsight. Secondary sources (S24, S26) say his father talked him into it ("I'm gonna see how far I can ride this thing"); if so, deference to a trusted figure also played a part (also Six-consistent, but unverified). Many people would describe a big career leap as fear.

claims.claim: When Warner Bros. wanted him for Superman, his idea was a hero who "has become almost afraid of himself and his own power"; he says the studio "didn't really want a fear-based character at the centre of their movie", and he walked away.
claims.inference: What he found psychologically true in the most invincible character in fiction was fear. Gilbey (S02) reads it as "a metaphor for what was happening at the time in his own life"; that is the writer's interpretation.
claims.alternative: An actor's craft pitch, not a confession; single source; told in 2020 about the early 2000s.

claims.claim: He turned down Superman more than once in the early 2000s, and his stated reasons shifted over two decades: fulfilment (2003), "I didn't ever want to do it" (2004), "Superman was a risk" (2021), and "I just didn't want my life to be swallowed up by my work" (2024).
claims.inference: Turned down "twice" per S01 and NPR (S14). The constant beneath the changing reasons is refusal of a long studio commitment that would define him. The "$100m" fee is "industry gossip" (S07); do not state it.
claims.alternative: A shrewd career call explains it; so does a Seven's fear of being trapped or a Nine's fear of being swallowed. The reasons are partly retrofitted to each interviewer.

claims.claim: The story that he turned down Batman is disputed: in 2015 he told Playboy he had "said no to some of the wrong people" and was "so scared of being considered only one thing", then clarified that Warner Bros. "wanted me to talk about Batman. I wanted to talk about The Prestige"; Christopher Nolan said in 2023 "It never got that far" and that Hartnett was more interested in The Prestige.
claims.inference: Nolan (S21) and Gilbey (S02, "a conversation with Christopher Nolan") agree there was no offer. Hartnett's own versions consistently name fear of typecasting ("my fear of the concept of being one thing in my career and one thing only", S23). S01 and S12 misplace the conversation at The Dark Knight; Nolan ties it to his first Batman casting (Batman Begins, 2005).
claims.alternative: Do not write that he turned down Batman. Say he met Nolan about it and steered toward The Prestige, which Nolan cast with Christian Bale. The Playboy quotes are secondhand (S24); the Playboy original (S32) was not opened.

claims.claim: Interviewing him at 23 in 2002, Rachel Cooke saw a young man "so gauche and anxious" who "looks flustered" and checked himself mid-answer ("tell me if it's bullshit"), and who added praise for Tom Cruise "perhaps afraid that he might sound as if he is dissing Cruise".
claims.inference: A contemporaneous outside observation of anxious self-monitoring at the peak of his fame.
claims.alternative: Junket nerves at 23; Cooke's "perhaps afraid" is her reading. The 2003 writer (S04) similarly saw "a schoolboy taking an oral exam", a second outside impression in the same register.

claims.claim: In 2002 he described himself as contrarian toward his advisers: "I'm one of those people who when someone says 'turn right,' go left."
claims.inference: Reflexive testing of authority is a classic counterphobic Six marker; the same posture shows up in the Purchase letter (C07), the studio fights (C25) and testing Malarek (C23).
claims.alternative: Bravado for a journalist; also fits Eight or Four. He undercuts it with "I don't know whether they've figured that out yet...".

claims.claim: In 2002 he said he respected people "who recognise their boundaries as to how much of this stuff they can take" and that he had "a pretty good bullshit meter".
claims.inference: Vigilance toward inauthenticity and an explicit boundary model for fame, at 23.
claims.alternative: Ordinary self-protective talk from a young star; also Five-consistent (boundaries).

claims.claim: The same 2002 interview holds the strongest early evidence against a vigilant reading: "I just kind go along for the ride ... someone like me can just wander through", "People care about my fame, not me", and "I'm not interested in fighting the publicity machine," followed by "That's not my fight."
claims.inference: This is the Nine case in his own words: drift, self-effacement, declining the fight. It is the main counterevidence to the Six reading.
claims.alternative: In the same breath he adds "There are other things I want to fight for. I want interesting roles. I want to do some good in the world"; the self-effacement may be Midwestern modesty rather than self-forgetting.

claims.claim: In 2003 he said Minneapolis was where he could "be myself", and described Los Angeles as a place where "You're either an outsider looking in or an insider stuck inside this expensive ball of wax."
claims.inference: Home and old friends as the place of safety and identity, already at 24; consistent with 2021-2024 accounts (C28, C29).
claims.alternative: Common to many actors who keep a home base.

claims.claim: Accounts of his relationship with Harrison Ford on Hollywood Homicide (2003) conflict: at the 2003 junket he called Ford "my idol" and said "It was a little bit intimidating at first but eventually we got along very well"; a later compilation quotes him saying Ford "tested me and I hated him for a while".
claims.inference: The only primary source opened (S04) is warm. The harsher quote (S24) has no traceable original.
claims.alternative: Do not use the "hated him" line. If used at all, quote S04.

claims.claim: After Black Hawk Down and the Pearl Harbor and 40 Days publicity, he stepped away for about 15 to 18 months, moved back to Minnesota and parted from his agents, without quitting acting; in 2004 he said he had spent the time "wondering, 'Who am I? What do I want to be when I grow up?'" and might "hermit myself away" to paint.
claims.inference: His contemporaneous number is 15 months (S05, 2004); S01 (2024, writer) and S24 say 18. He planned "time off" in April 2002 (S03). He repeatedly insists he never stopped working (S06 2014: "joined a cult or something ... I was doing work I thought was worthy"; S09; S14).
claims.alternative: Circumstance (burnout after four years of nonstop work, S03) explains the break as well as any type. Say about a year and a half, or more than a year, rather than a month count.

claims.claim: In 2004 he said "trying to stay at the top is a shortcut to unhappiness", and in 2021 that "the guys who are on top are terrified that someone's coming up behind them ... you're going to spend your whole life looking over your shoulder. I never wanted that."
claims.inference: He describes the top of the industry as a state of permanent vigilance he refused to live in. A Six who knows how a threatened position feels would describe it this way; so would anyone who watched it.
claims.alternative: Observation of others, not self-report of his own fear; Nine (peace) and simple values explain it too.

claims.claim: Quoted from a 2014 Details interview about the peak years: "I was on the cover of every magazine ... I couldn't really go anywhere. I didn't feel comfortable in my own skin. I was alone. I didn't trust anyone."
claims.inference: If accurate, he names isolation and distrust as the state that drove the retreat: central to the Six reading.
claims.alternative: Secondhand only (Details via Us Weekly via PopCulture, S25; El País, S24, omits "I didn't feel comfortable in my own skin"); the Details original (S31) was not opened. Fame, stalking (C33) and press hostility (C26) are sufficient situational causes. Quote only with attribution to Us Weekly's report of the Details interview, or paraphrase.

claims.claim: He measures projects partly by whether someone will see them through: he took Penny Dreadful partly for the guarantee it would be marketed (2014), and in 2026 defined success as approaching projects "with an openness and have the knowledge that it will be released in a good way".
claims.inference: A repeated security criterion across 12 years: assurance that the system behind a project will hold. Six-consistent.
claims.alternative: Any actor burned by unreleased independent films wants distribution; professional incentive. The 2014 "guarantee" sentence is the AP writer's paraphrase.

claims.claim: Before playing journalist Victor Malarek in Target Number One he met him, he said, because "I wanted to see if he was full of shit."
claims.inference: Testing a person's authenticity before committing: the Six's test-before-trust, stated plainly. He adds "My interest in going to meet him was not to have flowers laid at my feet."
claims.alternative: Standard research for playing a real person, phrased as a joke.

claims.claim: Days after a 2020 Guardian interview, he phoned the journalist because he did not feel he had made his feelings about Harvey Weinstein clear, then said "I wasn't surprised he was a creep ... But I guess I was surprised at the extent of his creepiness"; he declined to claim harassment himself ("That's not my experience and it's not my place to claim that").
claims.inference: An observed behaviour reported by Ryan Gilbey ("He is nothing if not conscientious"): unprompted worry that his words would land wrongly, followed by correction. In 2015 he said the same about press in general: "you have to be cautious about how you put certain things" (S23). Six (or One) conscientiousness; not a Nine's letting it slide.
claims.alternative: Prudence on a sensitive subject, possibly advised by a publicist. Weinstein is a convicted sex offender; keep Hartnett's words attributed and do not imply he alleges abuse.

claims.claim: He had open friction with powerful institutions early: an "antagonistic relationship" with Dimension/Miramax over contract extensions, and studios that "looked at me as someone who had bitten the hand that fed me"; "I burned my bridges at the studios because I wasn't participating."
claims.inference: Counts against a conflict-avoidant Nine: he names antagonism and its cost. The 2021 chewing-gum anecdote (S07) shows the control dispute in miniature.
claims.alternative: He frames it as non-participation rather than rebellion ("I wasn't doing it to be recalcitrant or a rebel"), which a Nine's passive resistance would also produce.

claims.claim: He called the 2001 Vanity Fair cover story "The Making of Josh Hartnett" "an awful piece" that made people think "I'd been thrust on them"; on rereading it in 2020 he said it was "a set-up-to-fail moment" and that he had felt "'Oh my God! I'm not the tallest poppy yet – don't cut me down!'"
claims.inference: Anticipating attack before he had even risen: threat expectancy, Six-consistent. Also shows him revising a harsh judgment after checking ("realised it wasn't so bad after all").
claims.alternative: Any young star would dread such hype; the Vanity Fair piece itself (S33) was not opened, so its contents are known only secondhand.

claims.claim: In 2021 he summed up the retreat with "I decided to have a life," then "To put that first. That was always my goal," explaining that friends and family "make me who I am" and that he felt "completely comfortable being with the people I knew liked me before I was making films".
claims.inference: He chose the security of proven, long-standing loyalties over status. The phrase "liked me before" is about trustworthiness of affection, which fits Six; belonging and comfort also fit Nine.
claims.alternative: A values statement any family-minded person might make; writer frames it as "honesty and integrity".

claims.claim: He says achievement did not satisfy him and community did: "after a certain amount of time chasing a goal, I realized that achieving these things wasn't giving me back the satisfaction I hoped it would ... the thing that really holds you is your community. I felt that I was kind of rootless at that time."
claims.inference: Belonging as the foundation that "holds you"; echoed in Men's Health 2024 via Fox (S29): without "a good stable background of good community and good family, it doesn't really amount to much". Counts strongly against Three; Six (security in group) or Nine (connection).
claims.alternative: Midlife reflection by a father of four; partly a response to the interviewer, a friend from O.

claims.claim: Across 2024-2026 he explains the retreat as protecting a self that others were defining: "I felt like I hadn't defined myself yet ... people ... putting their definition of me out there ... was affecting my own idea of who I am ... I am less afraid of other people's opinions" (2026), and "all these other opinions of who I was constantly swirling around in the miasma that is my brain ... it was self-protective" (2024).
claims.inference: The central self-explanation, repeated to six outlets. Note the vocabulary: protection, intrusion, "afraid of other people's opinions", "you're forced to either fight against or go along with people's perceptions" (S08). He frames the problem as threat to an unformed self, not as a wish to be unique (against Four) or as numbness (against Nine).
claims.alternative: A standard developmental story about early fame, prompted by interviewers; Four (identity) and Nine (losing self in others' agendas) both read the same words differently. The "frontal lobe" line (S09) shows he partly explains it by age, not type.

claims.claim: He describes loss of control to the industry as what frightened him and regaining a say as relief: "I didn't want to feel like I wasn't in any control of my own life" (2026); "I didn't want someone else dictating how I was portrayed" (2024); being executive producer on Below was "really relieving" because otherwise "they have complete control over the work you've done" and "That's terrifying" (2026).
claims.inference: Control sought as relief from fear, not as dominance: that separates a Six reading from an Eight one. HuffPost 2017 via AnOther (S26): "didn't feel like I was totally in control of my own destiny" (secondhand).
claims.alternative: Every actor resents losing the edit; "terrifying" is partly idiom.

claims.claim: He now chooses work by trust: "It's about finding people who you really trust" (2024); "first off, you need to have good people that you're working with" (2026); Lucky Number Slevin was a favourite "because that was all friends"; and he said in 2018 that when he connects with someone "on an intellectual level, I just want to go and do something with them".
claims.inference: McGurk (S01) calls it "his new rule: work with people you trust". He reorganized his career around trusted relationships after the Batman-Prestige episode, which he describes as a missed relationship (S23).
claims.alternative: "It's all about directors" (his own phrase in 2024, S09) is common actor talk and good career strategy; Five (intellectual connection) and Nine (harmony) also fit.

claims.claim: Christopher Nolan, whom he had met two decades earlier, cast him as Ernest Lawrence in Oppenheimer (2023); Hartnett said "the implication was: 'I'd better take it.' You only get so many opportunities with Chris Nolan" and "I recognise the missed opportunity to work with a guy like Chris."
claims.inference: Shows the recalibration from avoiding typecasting to valuing trusted relationships (C31).
claims.alternative: None on the facts.

claims.claim: He says that at the height of his fame people showed up at his house and stalked him, and that when he was 27 "a guy showed up at one of my premieres with a gun, claiming to be my father. He ended up in prison"; he prefaced it "I don't want to give this a lot of weight" and concluded "I wasn't going to be grist for the mill."
claims.inference: A real threat gives a situational reason for vigilance and retreat. That he minimized it is notable: he refuses to make the frightening story the explanation.
claims.alternative: Unverified beyond his account; the man is unnamed and no court record was found. This is circumstance, not type: it explains security-seeking without any Enneagram motive. Attribute; do not add detail; do not present the man as an armed stalker as established fact.

claims.claim: He describes himself as a worrier from childhood: "My family says I was an existentialist from the age of 12."
claims.inference: Family testimony relayed by him. McGurk introduces it with "A natural worrier", which is the writer's phrase.
claims.alternative: A family joke about a thoughtful kid; single source.

claims.claim: At the 2018 British Independent Film Awards he said he gets "a lot of anxiety about these sort of events because I have to go up on stage and read", adding that he could never be a presenter.
claims.inference: Specific performance anxiety when he must appear as himself rather than in character; consistent with "I clam up around really fantastic filmmakers and writers" (2026, S18).
claims.alternative: Common stage nerves, not a condition. The video's title ("suffers from anxiety") overstates it. Machine transcript, two models agree; re-listen at about 2:07.

claims.claim: Offered the lead in Trap (2024), he said his first thought on reading the script was "Oh my God, if this goes wrong, it's all on me", then "I love challenges"; on Q he said if the character didn't work "the whole film fails".
claims.inference: Anticipates the failure scenario first, then commits: the same fear-then-act shape as Pearl Harbor (C09).
claims.alternative: Normal lead-actor pressure, told with a laugh on a press day.

claims.claim: Directed by Oliver Stone on a loosely autobiographical film (White Lies, shot in 2026 and unreleased when he described it in August-October 2026), he says Stone kept him off balance by complimenting everyone but him, that he "so badly wanted to please him", and that Stone got the performance "by playing off my own insecurity".
claims.inference: Under a withholding authority he reports insecurity and an intense wish to please, and he pushed harder: the Six's relationship to authority in a single anecdote.
claims.alternative: A director's deliberate technique works on many actors; Two or Nine wishes to please also fit. Machine transcript (S18; two models agree); re-listen at about 20:34-20:54.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck the title and release of the Oliver Stone film (S15 names it White Lies) when it is announced or released.

claims.claim: Fear vocabulary persists into his late forties, often half-joking: the Verity-Below release week "feels simultaneously terrifying ... this might be the last time we speak"; comparisons to Widow's Bay were "a little bit of a scary situation if we get caught in that flywheel of people's opinion"; the cast were "terrified" of the Newfoundland accent.
claims.inference: Recurring threat framing around other people's opinions and outcomes he cannot control.
claims.alternative: Much of this is idiom and comic exaggeration; weigh it lightly.

claims.claim: M. Night Shyamalan says he cast Hartnett because he was "a bona fide movie star, that's a great human being and is willing to risk everything", and recalled Hartnett telling him that "danger is what really drives him".
claims.inference: A collaborator's view of him as a risk-taker. The "danger" line is Shyamalan's recollection of Hartnett's words, reported via a GQ video by TheWrap (S22).
claims.alternative: Promotional praise; secondhand for the danger line. Supports counterphobic Six, Seven or Eight equally.

claims.claim: He has a thrill-seeking streak: he says he "used to track-race Porsche cars all the time" and took a Bugatti onto an F1 track in Kuala Lumpur; in 2003 he called his appeal "my drive to explore things, my desire to experience the world"; and Shyamalan recalls him saying "danger is what really drives him" (C39).
claims.inference: Unexplained by a security-seeking reading unless it is counterphobic risk-taking or a Seven wing.
claims.alternative: Seven is the type this best fits; a wealthy young man racing cars is also just circumstance. Reports that he did his own stunts on Fight or Flight (2025) were seen only in search summaries and are not in this record; omit unless sourced.

claims.claim: He disowns self-focus: talking about his own career "feels too isolating, and it's self-indulgent" (2024); family "don't allow me the time to be self-indulgent" (2024); and he asked for his Below character not to be "constantly talking about his trauma", citing a Minnesotan "reticence ... to complain about their own situation" (2026).
claims.inference: Counts against Four, whose motive centres on the significance of personal feeling.
claims.alternative: Midwestern norms and good screen-writing instinct, not motive.

claims.claim: He lives in the Hampshire countryside with his wife, the English actor Tamsin Egerton (together since the early 2010s, married November 2021), and their four children, plus pygmy goats, chickens and guinea pigs; on a UK marriage visa he can work abroad about 180 days a year, which, McGurk writes, "also suits him fine", and he says of village life that "nobody cares" about his career.
claims.inference: Current settled life chosen for privacy and family. "I like being the outlier" and "The goats are more my vibe" (S08) are his jokes about being the only American in an English household.
claims.alternative: Family location follows his wife's parents and the pandemic (S02, S12), not only his temperament. Do not name or gender the children (kept private, S29).
claims.review_trigger: Update if residence, family size, marital status or visa arrangement changes; recheck at each refresh.

claims.claim: He returned to studio work around 2020-2021 partly because "we had a couple of kids, so I wanted to establish something that was a little bit more solid", starting with Guy Ritchie's Wrath of Man (2021) and leading to Operation Fortune and Black Mirror's "Beyond the Sea" (2023), Oppenheimer (2023), The Bear (2024) and Trap (2024).
claims.inference: A security motive for the comeback in his own words.
claims.alternative: Parenthood and money are sufficient explanations; the Six reading should not lean on this.

claims.claim: As of October 22, 2026, he co-stars as Jeremy Crawford in Verity (US release October 2, 2026) and leads Netflix's six-episode Below (October 8, 2026), on which he was also an executive producer and which drew 21.2 million views in its first full week.
claims.inference: Current-accuracy check; use only if it deepens the argument (e.g. the "terrifying" release week, C38).
claims.alternative: None on the facts.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck viewing figures, any Below season-two decision and later releases at the next refresh or by 2027-10-22.

claims.claim: On September 25, 2025, during the Below shoot, he was a passenger in an SUV that collided with a Royal Newfoundland Constabulary patrol car in St. John's; both men in the SUV were taken to hospital with what police believed were minor injuries. Hartnett later said a police car "running a red light" T-boned them and that he kept it quiet because "I didn't really want it to be the story."
claims.inference: The fault account is his; police said they were investigating and sought witnesses. His choice not to publicize it fits his privacy pattern.
claims.alternative: Do not state fault as fact. No investigation finding was located.
claims.review_trigger: Check for an RNC finding, charge or civil claim before any refresh that mentions the crash.

claims.claim: He also describes contentment and stillness: of country life, "the quiet, the still; all of it", and of four children, "In a way, less is happening. But more of the important stuff is happening"; moving to the UK "didn't feel unnatural".
claims.inference: The Nine reading's best recent evidence: settledness and ease.
claims.alternative: Settling into parenthood in one's forties explains this for any type; a Six can find security and relax.

claims.claim: He keeps his children away from the industry: in 2018 he wanted them "as unadulterated as possible", and in 2024 said "my kids don't really understand what I do".
claims.inference: Protective parenting consistent with his own account of what fame did to him.
claims.alternative: Common among actor-parents.

claims.claim: He has said the industry's pigeonholing was his main fear as a young actor: "I was so focused on not being pigeonholed and so scared of being considered only one thing" (2015, via El País) and "because of my fear of the concept of being one thing in my career and one thing only" (2015, USA Today via ComicBook).
claims.inference: He names fear as the driver of his career avoidance; the fear is of being fixed in place by others (a Six worried about losing autonomy, or a Seven about being trapped).
claims.alternative: Both quotes are secondhand from 2015 press; originals (S32, S36) not opened.

claims.claim: Across 2002-2026 his explanations for his biggest choices repeatedly run through fear, trust and protection from other people's control: he audits choices for fear (Pearl Harbor), imagines Superman as afraid of his power, tests people and institutions (the dean, advisers, Malarek), names distrust and intrusion as what drove the retreat, and now chooses work by trusted relationships and relief at regaining control.
claims.inference: This is the profile's organizing inference for a Type 6 reading, held at medium confidence. It rests on his own words in at least eight interviews over 24 years and two outside observations (S03, S02).
claims.alternative: Fear language is common English and partly prompted by interviewers; real threats (stalking, C33; hostile press, C26; studio pressure, C25) supply situational causes; and the 2002 "go along for the ride" and recent stillness (C16, C46) fit Nine. See type_hypothesis.

type_hypothesis.against: (1) His own 2002 words are the Nine's: "I just kind go along for the ride ... someone like me can just wander through" and "That's not my fight" (C16); his recent life is described in Nine terms too: "the quiet, the still" and "less is happening. But more of the important stuff is happening" (C46). (2) The central motion of his story is withdrawal from overwhelm to home, family and stillness (C19, C42), which Nine (and Five) explain as naturally as Six. (3) He rarely presents as anxious now: the 2020-2026 interviewers describe him relaxed, warm and joking (S08, S12, S18), and most of his recent fear words are comic idiom (C38). (4) The explicit anxiety evidence is narrow: stage nerves at award events (C35) and a family joke about being "an existentialist from the age of 12" (C34); "a natural worrier" is the writer's phrase. (5) Two of the strongest fear-and-distrust quotes are secondhand (Details 2014, C21; Playboy and USA Today 2015, C48). (6) Situational causes are heavy: stalking and a man with a gun at a premiere (C33), a hostile press (C26), studio pressure and contract options (C25), and four years of nonstop work (C19); a vigilant style could be learned from circumstance rather than driven by type. (7) He raced cars, told Shyamalan danger drives him, and seeks work that is "new and surprising" (C39, C40, S14), which a security-seeking type does not predict unless counterphobic. (8) His identity language ("defined", "more myself", "the outlier", C29, C42) is also the Four's vocabulary.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 9 is the strongest rival. The shape of his life is a Nine's: overwhelmed by the noise of fame he did not fight it so much as leave it, going home to Minnesota for about a year and a half (C19), and for two decades he has preferred family, old friends and a quiet village to status (C27, C42, C46). His explanations stress being swallowed and losing himself to other people's agendas: "I just didn't want my life to be swallowed up by my work" (C11); others' definitions were "affecting my own idea of who I am" (C29); "you're forced to either fight against or go along with people's perceptions of you" (C29). He disclaims ambition and self-importance ("I'm not any more important than anyone else", "go along for the ride", C16), credits a father who did not value achievement (C04), and now describes contentment and stillness (C46). His resistance is the Nine's kind: he says he was not "recalcitrant or a rebel"; he just "wasn't participating" (C25). Type 4 is live for the outsider and identity language (Huck Finn, "the outlier", "more myself", "the explorative artist that I wanted to be", C06, C29, C42) and the painter's self-image, but he disowns self-focus and complaint (C41) and grounds identity in community rather than distinctiveness (C28). Type 7 is live for variety-seeking, car racing, "danger" and the fear of being "pigeonholed" or locked into a long Superman deal (C11, C40, C48), but when it mattered he chose stillness and duty over options (C42, C43). Type 5 was considered for privacy, boundaries and "hermit myself away" (C15, C19) and set aside because he locates safety in people, not in withdrawal into the mind. Type 8 was considered for the contrarian and control streak (C14, C30) and set aside because he frames control as relief from fear, not as power. Same-cluster caution: the site types other walked-away actors Brendan Fraser and Keanu Reeves as 9, so readers will expect leaving Hollywood to mean Nine; the profile must show why that does not fit here.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What he does under pressure, and how he explains it. A Nine keeps the peace inside himself: he numbs out, lets things slide and, when pushed, withdraws or quietly digs in, and his account of hard choices centres on comfort, harmony and not being disturbed. A Six scans for threat, tests authorities and recruits trusted allies, and explains hard choices through fear, trust and protection. Hartnett's record leans Six on four observable points. (1) He audits his own decisions for fear and acts against it: Pearl Harbor "would've been based on fear. Then it defined me, which means I was right to fear it" (C09); Trap, "if this goes wrong, it's all on me", then "I love challenges" (C36); Superman imagined as a hero "afraid of himself and his own power" (C10). (2) He tests rather than smooths: a letter to the dean at 18 (C07), "when someone says 'turn right,' go left" (C14), "I wanted to see if he was full of shit" (C23), and open antagonism with Miramax and the studios until he "burned my bridges" (C25). (3) He builds safety out of trusted people rather than out of being left alone: "I didn't trust anyone" at the peak (C21, secondhand), the people "I knew liked me before I was making films" (C27), "It's about finding people who you really trust" (C31), wanting the Below cast to come out "fully intact as a family" (S18). (4) He loops back on his own words when he fears they will be misread: the unprompted call about Weinstein (C24), "you have to be cautious about how you put certain things" (S23), and the 2002 observer's "perhaps afraid that he might sound as if he is dissing Cruise" (C13). Under a withholding authority he reports insecurity and a wish to please (C37); getting control back was "really relieving" because losing it is "terrifying" (C30). A Nine reading has to treat each of these as incidental; a Six reading predicts them. Limits: points (1) and (4) rest on about ten statements over 24 years; two fear quotes are secondhand (C21, C48); fear words are partly idiom; and stalking and press hostility supply situational reasons for vigilance. Confidence stays medium.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: (1) The 2002 "go along for the ride ... wander through" self-portrait (C16), which is pure Nine and was said at the moment he was preparing to step back. (2) The thrill-seeking: track-racing gutted Porsche 911s, a Bugatti on an F1 track, "danger is what really drives him" (C39, C40); counterphobia or a Seven wing would explain it, but neither is demonstrated. (3) Why he took Pearl Harbor against his fear but refused Superman (C09, C11): the fear audit predicts the first and not obviously the second, unless a decade-long commitment was the decisive threat. (4) How relaxed he now seems with the press while still reaching for fear vocabulary (C29, C38). (5) How easily he relocates (moving to the UK "didn't feel unnatural", C46) when a Six is often attached to familiar ground; his attachment seems to be to people, not place. (6) The Kerry-campaign regret and political worry reported secondhand or in passing (S24, S01), not explored. Wing unresolved (6w7 for humour, adventure and cars; 6w5 for privacy, homework and "intellectual" connection); no subtype attempted.
